newsitem.title: UK: Protestants to parade on IRA anniverary eve.
newsitem.headline: Protestants to parade on IRA anniverary eve.

text.p: Tension ran high in Northern Ireland on Saturday as Protestants planned to march on a Catholic church on the eve of the first anniversary of an IRA guerrilla bombing which ended a 17-month peace.

Police were drafted in to the Harryville suburb of the Northern town of Ballymena where Protestants planned a parade on a Catholic church mass which has been the focus of protest for more than 20 weeks.
The 96 percent Protestant community in Ballymena has picketed the church in protest at the refusal of Catholics in the nearby village of Dunloy to allow Protestants to parade there last summer.
Police said community leaders had agreed to postpone the parade until after the evening mass ends to avoid confrontation with worshippers.
Ian Paisley, the local member of parliament for the area, which is known as the Northern Ireland bible belt, said:"I don't think there will be any confrontation."
He and other members of the Protestant Unionist movement, which want the province to stay British, have condemned the protest and say all religious faith must be resepcted.

The protest has underlined tension between Northern Ireland's 40 percent Irish Catholic minority, which sympathises with efforts to reunite the province with Ireland, and the Protestant majority which wants it to remain British.

It is also viewed by security officials as a bad omen for the yearly Protestant marching season, a flashpoint period which starts officially on March 31 and which last year provoked the worst civil strife in the province for decades.

Last July police banned then allowed a Protestant Orange Order parade in the southern town of Portadown after Protestant protests across the province. The decision unleashed a wave of Catholic anger and polarised the already divided province.

Saturday night's parade is being staged almost a year after the February 9 bombing of London's Canary Wharf business complex by the Irish Republican Army which ended the guerrillas' 17-month truce and dashed hopes of lasting peace.

The IRA, which seeks to end British rule, has bombed security targets in Northern Ireland several times every week this year to back its demand that its political wing, Sinn Fein, be invited to Belfast peace talks.

It has failed to kill anyone this year but police say it is only a matter of time before the guerrillas claim their first fatality and provoke their Protestant Loyalist foes, who want the province to stay British, into ending their own ceasefire.

The IRA leadership briefed Dublin journalists on Friday to send a message that it will not restore its ceasefire unless Britain backs down on its demand that the IRA give up violence for good to earn a seat at Belfast peace talks.

An IRA leader said he could not forsee a new ceasefire until a strong government emerged after British elections due by May. Britain's Conservative government, facing certain defeat at the election, according to opinion polls, refused to budge.

"It implies that after the election it (the IRA) may be kind enough to announce another ceasefire. But by those words, they surely show themselves to be the blackmailers they are," Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew said.
